newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - T-bonds may sink deeper before bottoming.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - T-bonds may sink deeper before bottoming.

text.p: U.S. Treasury bond futures, which have been sliding steadily without a significant rebound since mid-February, probably have some more way to go before forming a viable base pattern, technical analysts said.
The market may well test its mid-1996 lows near 106 on a continuous chart-basis, which coincide with highs of about 7-1/4 percent in cash bond yield, in the near term, they said.
"The market is oversold, but the trend is down and there is still no base," said Terence Gabriel, a technical analyst at I.D.E.A. Inc. "It's still a 'sell rallies' kind of outlook."

"I think the reasonable thing would be to look for weakness down again to test the yield-highs from last summer," he said. "From there, I would expect a rally attempt, but there would have to be work done (to form a basing pattern)."
Gabriel said the 106-area contained a lot of Gann Line support and retracement levels, including a descending three-by-one Gann Line from the September 1993 highs now coming in at 105-30/32.
June T-bonds drifted narrowly on Monday, unchanged on the day at 106-20/32 at 1200 CDT/1700 GMT.

John Gambino of JBG Technical Analysis said the market could see a "tradable" rally of one or two points from the 106 to 107-area, given his Elliott Wave projection for an intermediate-term three-wave down move that started from December 1996 highs in the high-116s.

But he added that the longer-term outlook was bearish and that a break below 106 would lead to a fulfillment of a longer-term downward sequence that started from the December 1995/January 1996 highs. The third leg of that sequence started from the December 1996 highs.
"That would give you a count very, very close to 100 (in lead month futures)," Gambino said.
Gabriel warned that picking bottoms might not be worth the effort at this point, considering the strength of the market's decline and limited scope for a sizable bounce.
"We closed lower for eight consecutive weeks," he said of the overwhelming downward pressure.
Still, he noted that some positive factors were gradually gathering momentum, including oversold conditions and a shaky stock market.

"We have had a substantial upturn in relative strength, where the bonds are outperforming the S&P 500 index," Gabriel said. By late last week, the relative performance of bonds, which turned up in early April, had punched through a trendline drawn from January 1996, he noted.

"You're getting a relative-strength shift that probably suggests that bonds are benefiting somewhat from defensive money," he said, adding that continued weakness in stocks should render some support to bonds.
